stem: A nurse plans to obtain an oral temperature from a cooperative adult who has just finished drinking an iced beverage. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Wait 15 to 25 minutes after the beverage, then obtain the oral temperature using the usual sublingual technique.
options.B: Measure the oral temperature now and document the recent cold beverage so the reading can be interpreted in context.
options.C: Have the client rinse the mouth with room-temperature water, wait 5 minutes, and then obtain the oral temperature.
options.D: Obtain two oral temperatures immediately and average the readings to reduce the effect of the cold beverage on the result.

rationale: Open RN Nursing Skills states that recent hot or cold food or beverage intake can falsely raise or lower an oral temperature and recommends taking the oral temperature 15 to 25 minutes after such intake. Therefore A is correct. Documenting the recent drink does not make an immediately altered oral reading accurate. Rinsing and waiting only 5 minutes is not the cited timing for hot or cold intake, and averaging repeated immediate readings does not remove the same measurement artifact.
educational_objective: To reduce oral-temperature measurement error after hot or cold intake, wait the source-supported 15 to 25 minutes before obtaining the sublingual temperature.
source_organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Skills [Internet], 2nd edition, Chapter 1: General Survey
source_locator: Chapter 1 General Survey > Temperature > Oral Temperature: recent hot or cold food or beverage intake can produce falsely elevated or decreased readings; oral temperature should be taken 15 to 25 minutes following consumption of a hot or cold beverage or food.
source_claim_supported: Recent hot or cold intake can distort oral temperature measurement, and waiting 15 to 25 minutes before oral measurement improves accuracy.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed pp. 13 and 42: assess and respond to changes and trends in client vital signs; under Changes/Abnormalities in Vital Signs, apply knowledge needed to perform related nursing procedures and psychomotor skills when assessing vital signs.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — accurate oral temperature measurement
correction_summary: Rebuilt the distractors to remove absolute-word cueing and replaced generic route claims with realistic measurement errors. The revised item uses the directly sourced 15-to-25-minute interval and remaps the item to Reduction of Risk Potential, where NCSBN explicitly places vital-sign assessment procedures.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Vital-sign measurement — oral temperature accuracy after cold intake
audit_findings.stem: PASS — identifies the interfering factor and a client for whom the oral route is otherwise appropriate.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — exactly matches the source-supported waiting interval; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — documentation is appropriate but does not correct the known measurement artifact.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — rinsing may sound reasonable, but the cited guidance specifies 15–25 minutes after hot/cold intake rather than a 5-minute substitute.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — repeated immediate measurements share the same cold-intake distortion, so averaging does not correct the error.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — only A follows the directly cited technique and interval.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B, C, and D fail to allow the source-supported post-intake interval.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all option lengths are effectively equal and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential explicitly includes procedural knowledge for assessing vital signs.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether documentation, mouth rinsing, or averaging could compensate for a cold beverage; the source gives a direct 15–25-minute waiting rule, leaving A uniquely correct without unsupported precision.
